Primary standards

[edit]

The current approved version of (D)TLS is version 1.3, which is specified in:

  • RFC 8446 – "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3,"[7] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 9147 – "The Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Protocol Version 1.3,"[12] Proposed Standard.

The current standards replaces these former versions:

  • RFC 5246 – "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2,"[34] Obsolete.
  • RFC 6347 – "Datagram Transport Layer Security Version 1.2,"[9] Obsolete.
  • RFC 4346 – "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1,"[55] Historic.
  • RFC 2246 – "The TLS Protocol Version 1.0,"[197] Historic.
  • RFC 6101 – "The Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Protocol Version 3.0,"[198] Historic.
  • Internet Draft (1995): "The SSL Protocol"

Extensions

[edit]

Other RFCs subsequently extended (D)TLS.

Extensions to (D)TLS 1.3 include:

  • RFC 9367 – "GOST Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3,"[95] Informational.

Extensions to (D)TLS 1.2 include:

  • RFC 5288 – "AES Galois Counter Mode (GCM) Cipher Suites for TLS,"[96] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 5289 – "TLS Elliptic Curve Cipher Suites with SHA-256/384 and AES Galois Counter Mode (GCM),"[97] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 5746 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Renegotiation Indication Extension,"[119] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 5878 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authorization Extensions,"[199] Experimental.
  • RFC 5932 – "Camellia Cipher Suites for TLS,"[101] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 6066 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions: Extension Definitions,"[196] Proposed Standard.
    Includes Server Name Indication and OCSP stapling.
  • RFC 6091 – "Using OpenPGP Keys for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authentication,"[200] Informational.
  • RFC 6176 – "Prohibiting Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Version 2.0,"[28] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 6209 – "Addition of the ARIA Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[102] Informational.
  • RFC 6347 – "Datagram Transport Layer Security Version 1.2,"[9] Obsolete.
    The definition is now part of the DTLS 1.3 specification.
  • RFC 6367 – "Addition of the Camellia Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[100] Informational.
  • RFC 6460 – "Suite B Profile for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[201] Historic.
    Support for Suite B Cryptography has been discontinued by the National Security Agency.
  • RFC 6655 – "AES-CCM Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[98] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 7027 – "Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Brainpool Curves for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[202] Informational.
  • RFC 7251 – "AES-CCM Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for TLS,"[99] Informational.
  • RFC 7301 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation Extension,"[203] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 7366 – "Encrypt-then-MAC for Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS),"[147] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 7465 – "Prohibiting RC4 Cipher Suites,"[109] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 7507 – "TLS Fallback Signaling Cipher Suite Value (SCSV) for Preventing Protocol Downgrade Attacks,"[204] Obsolete.
  • RFC 7568 – "Deprecating Secure Sockets Layer Version 3.0,"[29] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 7627 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Session Hash and Extended Master Secret Extension,"[205] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 7685 – "A Transport Layer Security (TLS) ClientHello Padding Extension,"[206] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 8422 – "Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Versions 1.2 and Earlier,"[92] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 9189 – "GOST Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2,"[94] Informational.

Extensions to (D)TLS 1.1 include:

  • RFC 4366 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions,"[207] Obsolete.
    Describes both a set of specific extensions and a generic extension mechanism.
  • RFC 4492 – "Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) Cipher Suites for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[208] Obsolete.
  • RFC 4680 – "TLS Handshake Message for Supplemental Data,"[209] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 4681 – "TLS User Mapping Extension,"[210] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 4785 – "Pre-Shared Key (PSK) Ciphersuites with NULL Encryption for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[211] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 5054 – "Using the Secure Remote Password (SRP) Protocol for TLS Authentication,"[212] Informational.
    Defines the TLS-SRP ciphersuites.
  • RFC 5077 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Session Resumption without Server-Side State,"[193] Obsolete.
  • RFC 5081 – "Using OpenPGP Keys for Transport Layer Security (TLS) Authentication,"[213] Experimental.
  • RFC 5216 – "The EAP-TLS Authentication Protocol,"[214] Proposed Standard.

Extensions to TLS 1.0 include:

  • RFC 2595 – "Using TLS with IMAP, POP3 and ACAP,"[215] Proposed Standard.
    Specifies an extension to the IMAP, POP3 and ACAP services that allow the server and client to use transport-layer security to provide private, authenticated communication over the Internet.
  • RFC 2712 – "Addition of Kerberos Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[216] Proposed Standard.
    The 40-bit cipher suites defined in this memo appear only for the purpose of documenting the fact that those cipher suite codes have already been assigned.
  • RFC 2817 – "Upgrading to TLS Within HTTP/1.1,"[2] Proposed Standard.
    Explains how to use the Upgrade mechanism in HTTP/1.1 to initiate Transport Layer Security (TLS) over an existing TCP connection. This allows unsecured and secured HTTP traffic to share the same well known port (in this case, http: at 80 rather than https: at 443).
  • RFC 2818 – "HTTP Over TLS,"[217] Obsolete.
    Distinguishes secured traffic from insecure traffic by the use of a different 'server port'.
  • RFC 3207 – "SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security,"[218] Proposed Standard.
    Specifies an extension to the SMTP service that allows an SMTP server and client to use transport-layer security to provide private, authenticated communication over the Internet.
  • RFC 3268 – "Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Ciphersuites for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[219] Obsolete.
    Adds Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher suites to the previously existing symmetric ciphers.
  • RFC 3546 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions,"[220] Obsolete.
    Adds a mechanism for negotiating protocol extensions during session initialisation and defines some extensions.
  • RFC 3749 – "Transport Layer Security Protocol Compression Methods,"[221] Proposed Standard.
    Specifies the framework for compression methods and the DEFLATE compression method.
  • RFC 3943 – "Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Compression Using Lempel-Ziv-Stac (LZS),"[222] Informational.
  • RFC 4132 – "Addition of Camellia Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[223] Obsolete.
  • RFC 4162 – "Addition of SEED Cipher Suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[103] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 4217 – "Securing FTP with TLS,"[224] Proposed Standard.
  • RFC 4279 – "Pre-Shared Key Ciphersuites for Transport Layer Security (TLS),"[225] Proposed Standard.
    Adds three sets of new cipher suites for the TLS protocol to support authentication based on pre-shared keys.

Informational RFCs

[edit]
  • RFC 7457 – "Summarizing Known Attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS),"[226] Informational.
  • RFC 9325 – "Recommendations for Secure Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS),"[227] Best Current Practice 195.
